item.title: Connecticut council member sounds alarm after city opens law enforcement jobs to noncitizens
item.description: Danbury City Council voted 18-2 to let lawful permanent residents and DACA recipients join its police force, sparking a fierce citizenship debate.
item.content:encoded:
A Connecticut city opened its police force to lawful permanent residents and DACA recipients following an 18-2 city council vote, drawing pushback from one member who opposed the change.

"I don't think it is in any way intended to make our city feel safer," Danbury City Council member Candace Fay, a Republican, told "Fox & Friends First" co-host Todd Piro.

"There's no public policy reason behind what the council did. There's no overarching need for police officers in our city. There's no demand that this will meet. It was done simply as a political narrative, overwhelmingly done by virtue signaling, and it's further dividing our city," she added.

NEW MAINE LAW LIMITS POLICE COOPERATION WITH FEDERAL IMMIGRATION OFFICIALS

Fay's remarks come after the Danbury City Council voted last week to amend its police hiring ordinance, allowing lawful permanent residents and recipients of Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) to apply to become city police officers.

The change brings Danbury's rules in line with those adopted by Connecticut's Police Officer Standards and Training Council, which extended eligibility to lawful permanent residents in 2020 and DACA recipients in 2025.

Though neither the City Council nor Police Chief Patrick Ridenhour responded to Fox News' requests for comment before Tuesday morning's segment, city records show Ridenhour participated in an April committee discussion on the matter, during which he said police recruitment is a challenge and spoke about wanting to attract the "best qualified candidates."

Danbury Mayor Roberto Alves, a Democrat, said the measure removes barriers for qualified residents who want to serve the city.

HOCHUL BOASTS 'I JUST BANNED IT' AS NEW YORK OUTLAWS LOCAL POLICE PARTNERSHIPS WITH ICE

"(This) vote was about removing an unnecessary barrier for qualified people who already call Danbury home and want to serve their community," he said, per The Danbury News-Times.

City Council member Joe Britton, a Democrat, also defended the policy in the following statement:

"Danbury is an immigrant city and I believe someone who is lawfully here, committed to our community and willing to raise their hand and take an oath to protect and serve should have the opportunity to do so."

Fay, however, argued that U.S. citizenship should remain a requirement for officers entrusted with powers, including making arrests and using force.

"I'm asking for an objective standard. I'm asking that someone be a citizen. That's it," Fay said. "That's not overly egregious. It's not considering where they were born. It's not considering their ethnicity or even whether they're a good person," she continued.

"It is a reasonably objective standard whether they should be a citizen in order to be a police officer and enforce the state of Connecticut laws over citizens."

Fay also defended herself against accusations of racism over her opposition to the measure, saying her position was based solely on whether officers exercising police powers should be U.S. citizens.

item.title: Record gas prices squeeze Americans as summer travel season ends, midterms loom and Iran war wages on
item.description: Gas prices hit a record $4.15 per gallon over Labor Day weekend, shattering the previous high and posing a significant political test for Trump.
item.content:encoded:
As the summer travel season came to a close, Americans faced the most expensive Labor Day at the pump on record, extending the squeeze on household budgets for millions who hit the road over the holiday weekend.

AAA estimated that nearly 40 million Americans would drive over the holiday, paying unprecedented prices for gasoline.

The national average for regular gasoline reached $4.15 per gallon on Tuesday, up about 5 cents from the previous week and nearly 96 cents higher than a year earlier. The price shattered the previous Labor Day record of $3.82, set in 2012, and marked the first time the national average topped $4 during the holiday weekend.

FORGET GASOLINE: THIS OVERLOOKED FUEL COULD RAISE THE PRICE OF NEARLY EVERYTHING YOU BUY

The spike came despite a seasonal trend that typically brings some relief after Labor Day, when summer travel winds down and gasoline demand eases. This year, however, elevated crude oil prices tied to the Iran conflict offset that typical decline.

Fighting in the Middle East raised concerns about disruptions to oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow waterway between Iran and Oman that carries roughly one-fifth of the world's crude oil. Those concerns kept crude oil prices near $90 a barrel, limiting the seasonal decline in gas prices motorists typically see after Labor Day.

The record prices pose a political challenge for President Donald Trump, who campaigned on affordability and pledged to bring gasoline below $2 per gallon. His push to expand domestic oil and gas production has made energy costs a key test of his economic agenda, particularly as the Iran conflict drives crude prices higher.

With Americans still facing elevated everyday costs, record Labor Day gas prices could contribute to making affordability a major issue heading into the midterm elections in November.

TRUMP'S AMBITIOUS ENERGY BET COULD BE A WINNING HAND AS THE WORLD BURNS MORE OIL, GAS THAN EVER

While the national average reached $4.14 per gallon, prices varied significantly by state.

America's west was hit hardest. California had the nation's highest average gas prices at $5.78 per gallon, followed by Washington at $5.47, Hawaii at $5.41, Oregon at $4.98, Alaska at $4.96, Nevada at $4.91, Idaho at $4.62, Arizona at $4.52, Utah at $4.42 and Montana at $4.38.

At the other end of the spectrum, Indiana had the nation's cheapest gas at $3.44 per gallon. It was followed by Texas at $3.69, Oklahoma and Mississippi at $3.71, Louisiana at $3.75, Arkansas at $3.77, South Carolina and Kansas at $3.78, Alabama at $3.79 and Wisconsin at $3.80.

TRUMP JUST BROKERED A DEAL WITH THE COUNTRY SITTING ATOP THE WORLD’S LARGEST OIL RESERVES

With the summer driving season now over, drivers would typically expect prices to decline as fuel demand eases. But any relief at the pump will depend largely on whether crude oil prices retreat from recent highs or remain elevated by continued tensions in the Middle East.

The White House did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital’s request for comment.

item.title: Can the 'best showman in politics' deliver again? GOP bets on Trump at historic midterm convention
item.description: Donald Trump headlines the first-ever GOP midterm convention in Dallas, aiming to energize low-propensity MAGA voters ahead of key 2026 races.
item.content:encoded:
DALLAS — The stakes couldn’t be much higher for President Donald Trump and Republicans.

With less than two months until the midterm elections — and early voting just weeks away — Trump and the GOP descend on Texas starting Wednesday for the party’s first-ever midterm convention, as Republicans fight to keep control of Congress.

The GOP's playbook for the convention, which comes as Republicans face energized Democrats and political headwinds as they defend their slim House and Senate majorities, is to energize the party's base and boost turnout in key races that will determine control of Congress.

"We are putting the president on the ballot," Republican National Committee (RNC) Chair Joe Gruters emphasized in a Fox News Digital interview on the eve of the gathering. "That's exactly what we're doing with this midterm convention."

FIRST ON FOX: WHO'S SPEAKING - AND WHEN - AT THE GOP'S HISTORIC MIDTERM ELECTION

Democrats and Republicans traditionally hold large nominating conventions during presidential election years. However, Trump a year ago floated the idea of a similar gathering ahead of the midterms, to showcase the signature policy achievements he and the Republicans in Congress produced since he returned to the White House.

But Republicans are facing a low-propensity problem: MAGA voters who don't always go to the polls when Trump's name isn't on the ballot.

The GOP's solution: Hold what's been touted as a "Trumpapalooza."

"We have the best showman in politics in President Donald J. Trump," Gruters said. "He is the best vote getter for these little propensity voters. He's done it three times. He's going to deliver once again."

According to a speakers list, which was shared first with Fox News Digital on the eve of the convention, the president will deliver Wednesday's keynote address, which is tentatively scheduled to start at 9 p.m. ET.

Trump will return on Thursday evening to the American Airlines Center in downtown Dallas to close out the convention, with remarks after Vice President JD Vance gives the second night's keynote speech.

DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB

But the GOP is fighting political history, which has traditionally seen the party in power in Washington lose congressional seats during midterm election years. Add to that a challenging political climate fueled by persistent inflation Americans see at the grocery store, high gas prices tied to what polls show is an unpopular war with Iran, and Trump's negative approval ratings.

Gruters said, "In order to defy history, you've got to do things a little bit differently and that's why we're doing this Republican convention."

"We're going to use him where we can, where it's going to be advantageous," Gruters said of Trump. "We think that this midterm convention and what we're doing over the next couple of days will be just the start of some very exciting things over the next two months."

Democrats, obviously, see it differently.

"Democrats are going to win back power," Democratic National Committee (DNC) Chair Ken Martin predicted last month at the party's summer meeting as he looked towards the midterms.

The DNC, which remains in debt and decided against holding a similar convention, views the GOP gathering as an opportunity to criticize Republicans.

"While working families struggle to make ends meet in Donald Trump’s economy, Republicans are throwing a multi-million dollar party to celebrate Trump’s failing presidency," Martin argued in a convention eve statement. "Democrats are on the ground talking to voters about how to lower costs, expand affordable health care, and make life more affordable, offering real solutions while Republicans desperately attempt to paper over their billionaire-first agenda."

Democrats have also spotlighted the sizable number of Republican politicians who are staying away from the Dallas gathering.

Asked about the no-shows, Gruters said, "There's some people in tight races, they want to stay home. But listen, if you look at our speaker list, we have tons of those toss-up candidates that are here that are going to speak, that understand the value of the messaging and that we could deliver directly to the American people."

Midterm elections are often a referendum on the party in power, but Republicans aim to use the convention to draw a contrast as they spotlight Democrats' leftward lurch in this year's primaries and tie the party to far-left and socialist proposals.

SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

Gruters said speakers at the convention will ask Americans, "Do you want common sense and mainstream, or do you want the extreme left and these radicals that have been elected who fundamentally want to change our country."

"They want to fundamentally change the way you live at home," Gruters claimed as he referred to the Democrats.

The other part of the convention game plan is to showcase Trump's second-term achievements.

"He delivered for the American worker more so than anybody has over the last five decades," Gruters claimed. "Things like the Working Family Tax Cuts, the fair trade policies, the $19 trillion in investments that you're not going to feel right now today, but you will over time. Him constantly going to bat for the American worker, Trump RX accounts... This president understands what it takes and has empathy for what people are going through."

Also boosting the GOP: Money.

In the midterm battle, the RNC comes into the convention with a major campaign cash advantage over the DNC.

"We've been raising a lot of money. We've been saving that money," Gruters emphasized. "Now, over the next 60 days, you're going to see us spend that money to make sure we could turn out our voters, to make sure people know exactly where our candidates stand and where the opposition stands."

item.title: Traffic drama threatens to end Dem governor's tenure as voters head to polls in Rhode Island
item.description: Democratic Gov. Dan McKee could become the first elected governor in 12 years to lose renomination as Rhode Island's primary centers on a bridge crisis.
item.content:encoded:
Democratic Gov. Dan McKee of Rhode Island is fighting for his political life in the smallest U.S. state's primary elections on Wednesday as he faces potential downfall stemming from the nearly three-year partial closure of a crucial bridge.

McKee first assumed office in March 2021 when then-Gov. Gina Raimondo stepped down to become U.S. Commerce secretary. He was then elected four years ago for a full term. Now, McKee is trying to avoid becoming the nation's first elected governor in a dozen years to lose renomination.

The governor is facing off in a primary rematch with Helena Buonanno Foulkes, a former longtime executive with CVS, which is based in Rhode Island.

THESE 12 MIDTERM RACES WILL DECIDE WHICH PARTY CONTROLS THE SENATE

McKee narrowly edged Foulkes, who is the niece of former Democratic Sen. Chris Dodd of neighboring Connecticut, in a multi-candidate field in the 2022 Democratic primary before winning the general election in the solidly blue state.

As he fights for renomination, the governor has been outspent by a nearly two-to-one margin by Foulkes, according to Rhode Island campaign finance records.

Also working against McKee is his handling of the reconstruction of the Washington Bridge, which was shut in December 2023 after officials spotted critical structural flaws.

The bridge connects Providence to East Providence and before its westbound span was shut, it carried roughly 100,000 vehicles per day. Westbound and eastbound traffic share the reconfigured eastbound span with reduced lanes.

State officials originally estimated the bridge would reopen this year, but the completion date was later pushed back to November 2028.

The bridge has become a top issue in the gubernatorial primary, with McKee and Foulkes battling over the bidding process for reconstruction and the pace of rebuilding.

While pushing back on criticism over his handling of the bridge, McKee has slammed Foulkes as an out-of-touch corporate executive trying to buy herself an election win.

item.content:encoded:
After the 9/11 attacks 25 years ago, many Israelis declared, "We are all Americans now." As I wrote at the time, they had it backward: Americans had become Israelis. We had experienced the horror of Islamic terrorism that they had endured for decades.

Of course, that is only the beginning of our common cause with the Jewish people. They are a wellspring of the values upon which our country was founded. That is why every American should be troubled by the hatred toward Israel and American Jews that has festered inside our country since 9/11 and has been driven to new heights by the radical socialist left.

In New York, Democrat Mayor Zohran Mamdani has called the Jewish political advocacy group AIPAC "monsters." The Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), now the ascendant force in the Democratic Party, has made anti-Zionism a litmus test for membership. Hasan Piker, the streamer who has barnstormed for DSA candidates, recently said that "eventually someone’s going to come around and take action" against American Jews if they continue supporting Israel.

MAMDANI’S ANTI-ISRAEL AGENDA COMES AT NEW YORK’S EXPENSE

Indeed, it is already happening. FBI figures show anti-Jewish hate crimes have soared and now comprise 63% of all religion-based hate crimes, despite the fact Jews are about 2% of the U.S. population. The radical left offers outrageous excuses. In March, after a Hezbollah-inspired terrorist drove a truck loaded with gasoline and fireworks into a Michigan synagogue full of sleeping preschoolers, Abdul El-Sayed, the current Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate from Michigan, dismissed the attack by saying that "hurt people hurt people."

American Christians face a moment of reckoning: Will we stand with our Jewish compatriots, just as they stood with us 25 years ago? Will we speak frankly in their defense?

ISRAELI MEDICS TRAIN US SYNAGOGUES HOW TO RESPOND TO ATTACKS, AS HIGH HOLIDAYS APPROACH

We must. Our efforts to combat radical Islam and defend American values depend upon it.

We often speak of the Judeo-Christian principles that shaped our country, but we should remember the order of those words.

AMERICA AND ISRAEL: A COVENANT, NOT A CONTRACT

Christians alone did not invent the moral world from which Christianity emerged and on which America was founded. The tenets of Christianity are clearly based on the words of the prophets from the Old Testament. The God we worship is the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. The commandments we teach were given at Sinai. The language that shaped the American conscience was largely from the prophets of Israel.

The Hebrew Scriptures taught the principles that our Founders considered self-evident: that every human being bears the image of God, and that even the king answers to a higher moral law. These ideals reached our founding generation through Christianity, but not exclusively.

THE BEDROCK OF AMERICAN LIBERTY WAS LAID IN JERUSALEM

In 1790, the members of the Hebrew congregation of Newport wrote to President George Washington to seek assurance that Jews would enjoy the full rights of citizenship in the new nation. Washington answered that this country recognizes the "inherent natural rights" of the Jewish people. The government "gives to bigotry no sanction, to persecution no assistance." Then he quoted Micah, "everyone shall sit under his own vine and fig tree, and none shall make him afraid." (Micah 4:4)

Washington was affirming that Jews are equal beneficiaries of America’s promise and protection. Their belonging does not depend, as the far-left asserts today, upon holding fashionable opinions about the Middle East. It is guaranteed in our founding documents.

BILL MAHER BLASTS DEMOCRATIC PARTY, SAYS IT IS FINE WITH RELIGION 'AS LONG AS THAT FAITH ISN’T JEWISH'

The socialists are quick to assert that "anti-Zionism is not the same as antisemitism." They are wrong. To hold American Jews responsible for the policies of Israel is antisemitism. To target a synagogue is antisemitism. To treat "Zionism" as a sinister ethnic category is obvious antisemitism. And to warn Jews that they are in danger unless they sever an important part of their religious and cultural identity is antisemitism.

It is also anti-Americanism. There can be no embrace of American values without acknowledging and respecting the role of Judaism.

EXCLUSIVE: MEET THE MAN ISRAEL CHOSE TO BE ITS FIRST-EVER AMBASSADOR TO THE CHRISTIAN WORLD

That is why it falls to Christians to stand with our Jewish brothers and sisters. We share a moral inheritance. When Jews are driven from the public square, that inheritance is driven out with them. Jews and Christians are natural partners in defending the American promise. Only by working together can we make the self-evident truths as stated by our Founders once again self-evident in our culture.

Christians can treat the protection of our Jewish citizens as the responsibility of someone else, or we can treat it as necessary to our Judeo-Christian heritage. Only one of those is worthy of us.
